question: A 35-year-old man presents with 8 months of back pain, marked kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction, and a fluctuant swelling in the right iliac fossa. Which of the following BEST explains the finding in the iliac fossa?

answers.text: Psoas abscess from lower lumbar vertebral TB tracking along the psoas sheath to the iliac fossa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A cold abscess in Pott's disease of the lower thoracic or thoracolumbar spine typically tracks along the psoas muscle sheath and points in the iliac fossa (or groin/femoral triangle). This is the hallmark 'cold abscess' — no warmth, erythema, or acute tenderness.

answers.text: Haematogenous spread of TB forming a primary iliac fossa lymph node abscess

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Isolated iliac fossa TB lymphadenitis is uncommon; the classic explanation in a patient with Pott's disease and kyphosis is a psoas cold abscess tracking from the spinal focus.

answers.text: Pyogenic iliopsoas abscess secondary to Crohn's disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Crohn's-related psoas abscess is pyogenic, not the cold fluctuant swelling in this chronic TB presentation. The 8-month indolent course and gibbus strongly favour Pott's disease.

answers.text: Desmoid tumour arising from the iliacus fascia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A desmoid is a musculoaponeurotic fibromatosis — it would not explain the combination of spinal kyphosis and a fluctuant swelling in the context of a chronic constitutional illness.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pathogenesis of Pott's disease: vertebral body destruction → anterior paraspinal abscess → tracking along the psoas sheath → cold abscess pointing in the iliac fossa, groin, or femoral triangle. Gibbus = sharp angular kyphosis from anterior vertebral collapse.

Well done. Pott's disease of the lower thoracic/thoracolumbar spine is the most common spinal TB level. The cold abscess tracks along the psoas fascial sheath and presents as a fluctuant groin or iliac fossa swelling — a classic clinical trap in exams.
